paper_title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models have evolved from systems that primarily generate text into the foundation of AI agents that can carry out complex, multi-step tasks (Wang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2022; Agashe et al., 2025). By using tools, executing commands, modifying files, and interacting with external environments, these agents can translate user goals into concrete actions and observable outcomes (Schick et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). However, an AI agent relies on more than its underlying model (Sumers et al., 2023). Its behavior also depends on system instructions, context management, available tools, execution environments, persistent state, lifecycle controls, and safety mechanisms (Packer et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Mei et al., 2024). As result, the same model can behave differently when deployed through different system configurations. The agent harness connects the model to these surrounding components and determines what information reaches the model, which actions it can take, and how tool results, errors, and state changes are presented. Agent performance should therefore be understood as property of the complete system, with the harness treated as distinct and reliability-critical component (Li et al., 2026; Ning et al., 2026). Most existing agent benchmarks evaluate task completion through final answers, test results, or environment states (Merrill et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2025). These measures capture the combined effects of the model and its harness, but provide limited insight into whether specific harness mechanisms function reliably. As illustrated in Figure 1, task success may conceal lost context, misleading tool results, or lifecycle violations, while task failure can occur despite faithful harness execution. Even with the model held fixed, outcome-level comparisons alone cannot identify which harness behaviors account for the observed differences (Barke et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Recent studies have begun to examine harness configuration effects and safety, motivating complementary evaluation of individual harness mechanisms (Yao et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026). Such evaluation requires tasks that exercise explicit harness obligations, evidence that reveals whether those obligations were fulfilled, and separate assessments of harness behavior and task outcomes. Therefore, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, mechanism-oriented benchmark that treats the native agent harness as the system under test. It assesses harness behavior through auditable execution traces and external environment states. Building on an existing harness taxonomy (Li et al., 2026), we organize reliability into seven components: context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 tasks that exercise specific harness mechanisms through practical workflows, pairing explicit behavioral requirements with agent deliverables and executable or state-based ground truth. Cross-harness adapters preserve common task objectives and evaluation criteria while retaining each harnesss native interfaces and execution behavior. Evaluating the same modeltask combinations across harnesses provides basis for comparing their overall reliability and identifying weaknesses in individual components. Specifically, the Trajectory Tracing (TT) module reconstructs native execution records in shared Trace Intermediate Representation (Trace IR) while preserving their provenance. Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module combines these records with workspace artifacts and authoritative environment state to assemble criterion-specific evidence. After apparatus integrity checks, the two-layer evaluation framework separately assesses agent task performance and harness reliability. The Failure Attribution (FA) module then connects failed harness and agent criteria through predefined mechanism chains, with further evidence review required to distinguish activated candidate links from validated failure propagation. Across four harnesses, nine models, and 95 tasks, we evaluate 3,420 selected executions. Task success and harness-criterion satisfaction yield different harness rankings, and 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. These findings show how separate assessments of task outcomes and harness behavior expose reliability differences that outcome-only evaluation can overlook. Our contributions are summarized as follows. We construct TraceTrial-Bench, 95-task benchmark covering seven reliability components while preserving native harness behavior in cross-harness comparisons. We develop two-layer evaluation framework combining TT, MEA, and Trace IR to separately assess agent performance and harness reliability. We introduce failure attribution through explicit mechanism chains, distinguishing candidate links from failure propagation validated through evidence review. We evaluate four harnesses and nine models across 3,420 selected executions and provide tasks, configurations, traces, and verdicts for reproducible analysis. 2 Figure 1: Background and motivation. Agent performance depends on both the model and its harness, but task outcomes alone cannot distinguish model errors from harness shortfalls. TraceTrial-Bench uses native execution traces, artifacts, and environment state to assess agent performance and harness reliability separately and support evidence-based failure attribution.

sections.title: 2.1 Agent, Model, and Harness
sections.content: A modern agent combines models decisions with harness that manages repeated interaction with tools and the environment (Wei et al., 2026; Zhong & Zhu, 2026). We use the abstraction Agent = Model + Harness. (1) The model interprets available information and selects actions. The harness constructs context, exposes tool interfaces, transports calls and results, maintains persistent state, and enforces execution and permission controls. Tool calls, workspace changes, and output artifacts record the effects of this interaction. Task performance therefore depends on both model decisions and the way those decisions are supported by the harness. scaffold usually describes prompts, workflows, and action strategies built around the model, while runtime supplies processes, file systems, and computing resources. Our harness boundary includes their orchestration and control functions. External tool implementations, task environments, output artifacts, evaluators, and measurement apparatus remain outside that boundary. This separation is necessary when deciding whether an observation concerns harness obligation, an Agent decision, or failure of the measurement process.

sections.title: 2.2 Harness Reliability and Task Outcomes
sections.content: Harness functions affect several parts of an execution. Message selection, ordering, truncation, compaction, and session state determine which information remains available to the model (Ye et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). Tool inventories, parameter schemas, and routing determine the action interface (Hasan et al., 2026). Execution and lifecycle controls communicate command outcomes, manage long-running work, and preserve continuity across sessions and delegated tasks (Ma et al., 2026). Permissions and safety policies constrain the resulting actions (Bühler et al., 2026). Harness reliability concerns faithful information delivery and execution semantics. It does not guarantee task success: model can make an incorrect decision after receiving accurate information. Conversely, correct final artifact can coexist with an incomplete result channel, lost state transition, or violated interaction requirement. Evaluating only the final deliverable would combine these different situations into single outcome. 3 TraceTrial-Bench therefore assigns separate criteria to Agent outcomes and Harness obligations. The Agent layer checks required actions, task compliance, and final deliverables against authoritative state. The Harness layer checks whether the native system fulfilled the information and execution obligations exercised by the task. The seven-component taxonomy in Section 3.2.1 translates these responsibilities into observable properties.

sections.title: 2.3 Evidence Boundaries and Levels of Claim
sections.content: An external result, model-facing tool return, native session record, and normalized event are related observations, but they need not contain the same information. Environment state establishes what occurred. Changed artifacts identify the persisted deliverable, and native model-facing records establish what the model could observe. Provider-request evidence supports only the captured structured tool declarations, not uncaptured request bodies. Evidence from one boundary cannot automatically substitute for evidence from another. We distinguish four levels of claim. criterion verdict records satisfaction under the selected evidence. Confirming Harness defect additionally requires reconciliation with the authoritative sources for that criterion. An activated candidate link records failed endpoints and matching predeclared condition. Validating propagation further requires observable intermediate distortion, supported event order, and consideration of competing explanations. Apparatus failure is measurement limitation rather than Harness defect. These distinctions govern the scoring and attribution protocol developed next.

sections.title: 3 TraceTrial-Bench
sections.content: TraceTrial-Bench evaluates an agent harness as system, rather than treating it as transparent wrapper around model (Figure 2). The benchmark asks three distinct questions for every admitted run: (i) did the agent produce the required artifacts and actions, (ii) did the native harness preserve the information, execution semantics, and lifecycle behavior required by the task, and (iii) is an observed agent-side failure consistent with predeclared propagation mechanism from Harness-side criterion failure? The third question is addressed by automatically activating criterion-level candidate links when the corresponding Harness and Agent criteria both fail and the predeclared activation conditions are satisfied. This chapter describes the implemented measurement pipeline for the released runs. It combines apparatus admission, layer-specific Agent and Harness scoring, provenance-preserving trace reconstruction, deterministic criterion-specific evidence selection, and criterion-level candidate-mechanism linking. Runlevel outputs summarize criterion verdicts and automatically activated candidate links. These outputs support evidence-based failure analysis, while confirming Harness defects or failure propagation requires additional validation beyond automated scoring.

sections.title: 3.2.3 Harnesses and Cross-Harness Execution
sections.content: The release evaluates Codex, Claude Code, OpenClaw, and DeepSeek Harness through source-specific adapters. The runner freezes the task revision, harness adapter, requested and resolved model, reasoning setting, timeout, container image, judge model, and resource budgets. Each adapter launches the native harness and translates its observable records without replacing native prompt construction, tool transport, context policy, permissions, or session behavior. The task contract and oracle remain fixed while each harness retains its native execution strategy. Semantic equivalence permits representation normalization but prohibits changes that introduce capability, strengthen model-visible evidence, or alter task pass/fail conditions. The release manifest records the selected population and provenance of every run. Execution status, trace completeness, evaluation status, score, and attribution remain separate fields. Coverage is tracked separately for task assignment, native capability availability, mechanism activation, and evidence sufficiency. task can be present in the manifest without every selected execution exercising its target path. An unavailable named tool is not automatically defect if the native harness supplies an equivalent usable path. If an adapter cannot preserve the tasks domain semantics or required evidence, the corresponding comparison is non-comparable under the prospective protocol. The current experiments full-grid inclusion policy is stated separately in Section 4.3.

sections.title: 3.2.4 Execution Environment and Measurement Apparatus
sections.content: Runs execute in task-scoped containers with fixed container-internal workspace. The runner initializes frozen task state, captures private workspace baseline, and provisions deterministic task tools or stateful simulator services when declared. Task metadata controls user turns, tool calls, model calls, wall time, process containment, and other relevant resource bounds. The resolved configuration records the effective values. The measurement apparatus is isolated from the Agents writable output surface. Runner-owned lifecycle records, archive manifests, provider-request metadata, private simulator ledgers, baselines, and execution/security probes carry explicit provenance and digest bindings. The release manifest serves as the authoritative index connecting task, configuration, run identity, evidence, and checksums.

sections.title: 3.3.1 Trace Collection and Normalization
sections.content: Harness-specific trace acquisition. Native Harnesses expose different observability interfaces, so trace acquisition is implemented through source-specific adapters. The Codex adapter reads its JSON event stream. The Claude Code adapter combines stream-json output with the session record. The OpenClaw adapter reads local or gateway-backed JSON output together with session JSONL. The DeepSeek Harness adapter consumes its persistent JSON-RPC notification stream. Despite these interface differences, the archival policy is uniform. When native session or notification archive is available, the runner stores 7 redacted copy and its digest in the run archive. Valid records that cannot be normalized are preserved as provenance-tagged raw stdout or stderr events rather than discarded. Canonical event representation. To support comparison across Harnesses, the adapters map native observations to common event schema while retaining their source records. Optional type-specific fields are populated only when the native source exposes them. For tool interactions, tool_call records the requested action and tool_result records its correlated return. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We compare four native agent Harnesses over fully populated matrix of 95 tasks and nine model configurations. Each cell contains one selected execution and its final archived evaluation. The experiment asks whether outcome quality and Harness-criterion satisfaction vary together when the model and task population are held fixed. This section defines the data freeze and analysis protocol. Section 5 reports the results.

sections.title: 4.1 Evaluated Systems and Experimental Population
sections.content: Harnesses and models. The evaluated Harnesses are Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek Harness, and OpenClaw. Source-specific adapters provision the task and archive native evidence while retaining each Harnesss execution and tool-use interfaces. Task population. The analysis covers 95 tasks, each evaluated across all 36 modelHarness combinations. Taxonomy assignments are recovered from the task paths recorded with the runs and normalized as described in Appendix A.1: the four legacy ask-user tasks are assigned to Tools, while the task measuring truthful timeout and result handling is classified under Execution. sections.title: 4.2 Execution and Evaluation Configuration
sections.content: Execution environment and budgets. Runs execute in Docker with the task workspace mounted at /workspace. Task packages define the prompt or turn sequence, fixture, tools, expected deliverables, verifier, and resource limits. The recorded effective wall-time limits span 1205,400 seconds. The per-run resolved limit, rather than an example command or directory name, identifies the applicable execution budget. Task scheduling and recovery conditions vary across the collected runs. The present analysis consequently compares finalized functional outcomes and criterion verdicts. It does not interpret duration differences as controlled throughput experiment. Task-specific revisions and recovery runs also limit causal interpretations of difference between Harnesses. Fixed Judge identity. All 3,420 archived final evaluations use deepseek-v4-flash as the separate semantic Judge. The stored per-criterion output limits are 4,096 tokens in 1,966 evaluations, 8,192 in 1,452, and 32,000 in two. The raw criterion intersections contain 286 jointly clean runs, 1,065 Harness-only shortfalls, 369 Agent-only shortfalls, and 1,700 joint shortfalls. Thus 31.1% of all runs achieve Agent success despite at least one failed Harness criterion. Among the 1,700 joint-shortfall runs, 842 (49.5%) contain at least one stored candidate link, totaling 1,633 activated endpoint pairs. Of 2,069 Agent-failure runs, 1,773 (85.7%) retain at least one failed Agent criterion not reached by link. Joint failure is the largest state, but Harness and Agent verdicts frequently disagree. Claude Code has the most H-only runs, whereas OpenClaw has the most A-only runs and the most jointly clean runs (Figure 8(b)). The H-only state represents operational absorption: measured Harness shortfalls coexist 19 with fully passing Agent outcome. H-only runs therefore provide focused set of cases for diagnosing Harness-level shortfalls in tasks the Agent successfully completes. Co-occurrence is broader than candidate-link activation. Fewer than half of jointly failing runs contain stored link, and most Agent-failure runs retain at least one failed criterion not reached by any link. Conditional activation is lower in Execution and Governance than in Tools and Observability (Figure 8(c)). The table distinguishes this conditional rate from incidence over all runs: Harness can have more linked runs because it has more joint failures, without having higher conditional activation rate.

sections.title: 5.6 Recorded Resource Use
sections.content: At the frozen model-specific prices, mean estimated Agent costs per selected run are $0.436 for Claude Code, $0.595 for Codex, $0.446 for DeepSeek Harness, and $0.633 for OpenClaw. Mean total recorded tokens are 578.8k, 617.2k, 372.7k, and 680.0k, respectively. Table 7 retains the corresponding input, output, total-token, and cost columns for each model group.

sections.title: 5.7 Findings and Interpretation Limits
sections.content: The full-grid results support three conclusions. First, outcome quality and Harness-criterion satisfaction are empirically distinct: Agent success reaches 39.5%, but only 8.4% of runs pass every item in both layers, and different Harnesses lead the two aggregate measures. Second, differences depend on both the model and taxonomy dimension: within-model Harness macro ranges reach 16.2 points, and Harness micro orderings vary across dimensions. Third, failure co-occurrence exceeds candidate-link activation: 842 of 1,700 both-zero runs contain stored link, while 1,065 runs retain fully passing Agent outcomes despite Harness zeros. Appendix shows the task-level score grid, and Appendix provides five paired trajectory studies. These selected contrasts support inspection of specific behaviors rather than population-level estimate of attribution accuracy.

sections.title: 6.1 Limitations
sections.content: The evaluation uses targeted task suite with uneven mechanism coverage and one selected execution per task-model-harness combination. The results characterize the collected configurations, with limited evidence about generalization to deployment workloads or stability across repeated runs. Variation in task revisions, runtime settings, and scoring budgets further constrains causal conclusions about individual harness design choices.

sections.title: 6.2 Future Directions
sections.content: Harness Evolution. TraceTrial-Bench could support trace-guided improvement loop: identify mechanism failures, revise the relevant Harness behavior, and evaluate the changes on held-out tasks under fixed models and budgets. Controlled interventions and repeated executions would help assess whether each modification resolves the targeted failure and introduces regressions elsewhere. Tracking versions, configurations, and supporting evidence would connect Harness changes to measurable improvements in execution reliability and task performance. Evaluation for Recursive Self-Improvement. Future evaluation methods could combine task outcomes, Harness behavior, and evidence quality to provide actionable feedback for Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI). Crossed evaluations of Agent and Harness versions would help distinguish their individual contributions and interactions. Criterion-level feedback could then guide updates to Agent planning, tool use, and recovery strategies. Testing these updates on held-out tasks and unfamiliar Harnesses would assess whether the improvements transfer beyond the configurations used during adaptation.

sections.title: 7.1 Agent Harnesses
sections.content: Harness research addresses context, tools, state, verification, and permissions (Zhong & Zhu, 2026; Barbaste et al., 2026). ACE, ACDL, and SkillAlign improve context and interfaces (Zhang et al., 2026; Peleg Pelc et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026); LongHorizon-Harness and Crab address continuity and recovery (Ma 20 et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026); AgentBound and SafeHarness enforce policies and safeguards (Bühler et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026b). HARBOR, retrospective optimization, and SHAPER optimize configurations, skills, or harness code (Sengupta & Wang, 2026; Pan et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a), while HarnessFix diagnoses and patches implementation flaws (Chen et al., 2026). Interpreting improvements requires matched budgets and held-out evaluation (Wang et al., 2026b). TraceTrial-Bench supplies mechanismlevel criteria and evidence while preserving native harness behavior. Configuration search, skill evolution, and implementation repair target different system components. TraceTrial-Bench preserves native execution strategies and records obligation-specific evidence to examine whether task-level gains coincide with more reliable harness behavior.

sections.title: 7.2 Agent Evaluation and Failure Analysis
sections.content: Terminal-Bench and SWE-Bench Pro assess verifiable task outcomes (Merrill et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2025). Harness-Bench compares modelharness configurations under shared conditions (Yao et al., 2026), while HarnessAudit and HarnessRisk examine execution fidelity and adversarial risks (Liu et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026). For failure analysis, Who&When localizes responsible agents and error steps (Zhang et al., 2025). AgentRx diagnoses constraint violations (Barke et al., 2026), while REFLECT uses interventions and controlled replay (Lin et al., 2026a). TraceTrial-Bench complements these approaches by combining separate Agent and Harness criteria with evidence-based failure analysis. The two-layer evaluation exposes successful deliveries that coexist with Harness shortfalls. Its attribution framework connects failed criteria through declared mechanisms and source-specific evidence.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: TraceTrial-Bench evaluates native agent harnesses through 95 mechanism-oriented tasks across seven reliability components. Trajectory tracing and multi-source evidence support separate Agent and Harness scores, while explicit mechanism chains guide auditable failure analysis. Across 3,420 selected runs, Harness Macro differs by 12.2 percentage points and the leaders in task success and harness satisfaction differ. In particular, 1,065 of 3,420 runs (31.1%) achieve Agent success despite at least one failed Harness criterion. These successful deliveries with failed Harness criteria show that outcome-only evaluation cannot characterize harness reliability. The released tasks, configurations, traces, and verdicts support evidence-based comparison and diagnosis of harness behavior.

An adapter does not generate hidden reasoning, omitted tool results, approval decisions, or lost context. native compaction event records only the summary and boundary exposed by the harness, but it does not restore messages removed by the compaction process. 8. B.4 Semantic Equivalence and Eligibility This subsection defines prospective comparison requirements. It does not introduce an additional filter on the archived results in Section 5. Equivalent paths preserve the task goal, information, action opportunities, state effects, and evaluation conditions while leaving harness-controlled differences observable. 1. Goal equivalence. The model receives the same task objective, required deliverables, constraints, and success conditions. Formatting changes required by native input interface must not add, remove, or clarify task information. 2. Initial-state equivalence. The workspace, files, service records, credentials, environment variables, and simulated external state are initialized from the same task specification.
